# Desargues Involution Theorem and Isoconjugations

## Desargues Involution Theorem

:::{#thm-desarguesInvolutionTheorem}
## Desargues involution theorem, DIT
Let $A,B,C,D$ be four points on the conic $\mathcal{C}$, and let $\ell$ be a line not passing through $A,B,C,D$. Suppose that $\ell$ intersects $\mathcal{C}$ at points $X,Y$, then
$$
(X,Y),\,(AB\cap \ell,CD\cap \ell),\, (AC\cap\ell,BD\cap \ell),\, (AD\cap\ell, BC\cap\ell)
$$
is an involution.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Note that
$$
(X,Y;\ell\cap AB,\ell\cap AC)\stackrel{A}{=}(X,Y;B,C)_{\mathcal{C}}\stackrel{D}{=}(X,Y;\ell\cap DB,\ell\cap DC)=(Y,X;\ell\cap DC,\ell\cap DB)
$$
This shows that $(X,Y),(\ell\cap AB,\ell\cap CD),(\ell\cap AC,\ell\cap BD)$ is an involution. The same argument applies for the fourth pair.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
From DIT, given points $A,B,C,D$ (no three of which are collinear) and a line $\ell$ not passing through $A,B,C,D$, the map
$$
g:\mathbb{P}_\ell\to\mathbb{P}_\ell,\,X\mapsto\ell\cap (ABCDX)
$$
(where $\ell\cap (ABCDX)$ denotes the second intersection of $\ell$ and $(ABCDX)$) is an involution. From this viewpoint, it is natural to regard $\mathbb{P}_{AB}\cup\mathbb{P}_{CD}$ as a conic.
:::

:::{#cor-tangentConicsDit}
Given points $A,B,C,D$ (no three of which are collinear) and a line $\ell$ not passing through any of them, there are exactly two conics passing through $A,B,C,D$ and tangent to $\ell$ (the tangency points are the fixed points of the involution).
:::

:::{#thm-ddit}
## DDIT
Let $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4\in\mathcal{T}_\mathcal{C}$ be tangent to a conic $\mathcal{C}$. Set $\ell_i\cap \ell_j=A_{ij}$ for $1\leq i<j\leq 4$. Suppose that $P$ is not on $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4$, and $m,n$ are the two tangents to $\mathcal{C}$ passing through $P$, then 
$$
(m,n),(PA_{12},PA_{34}),(PA_{13},PA_{24}),(PA_{14},PA_{23})
$$
is an involution.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This is the dual of Desargues involution theorem.
:::

In Desargues involution theorem, the points $A,B,C,D$ need not be distinct, and a line becomes a tangent when they coincide. Dually, in DDIT, if two lines coincide, their intersection becomes the tangency point.

:::{#thm-carnot}
## Carnot theorem
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $A_1,A_2\in BC,\,B_1,B_2\in CA,\,C_1,C_2\in AB$. Fix point $P$ not on the three sides, then there exists a conic $\mathcal{C}$ intersecting the three sides of $ABC$ at $A_1,A_2,B_1,B_2,C_1,C_2$ if and only if
$$
\prod_{i=1}^2 A(B,C;P,A_i)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^2 B(C,A;P,B_i)\cdot  \prod_{i=1}^2 C(A,B;P,C_i)=1
$$
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that such a conic $\mathcal{C}$ exists, then we apply DIT to the quadrangle $B_1C_1B_2C_2\in\mathcal{C}$ and line $BC$,
$$
(A_1,A_2),(B,C),(B_1C_1\cap BC,B_2C_2\cap BC)
$$
is an involution, i.e.
$$
(B,C;B_1C_1\cap BC,A_1)\cdot (B,C;B_2C_2\cap BC,A_2)=1
$$
However, $(B,C;B_iC_i\cap BC,A_i)=A(B,C;P,A_i)\cdot A(B,C;P,B_iC_i\cap BC)^{-1}$, from Menelaus theorem,
$$
(B,C;B_iC_i\cap BC,A_i)=-A(B,C;P,A_i)\cdot B(C,A;P,B_i)\cdot C(A,B;P,C_i)
$$
for $i=1,2$. Multiplying these for $i=1,2$ yields Carnot theorem.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
The equality in Carnot theorem is equivalent to the existence of an isoconjugation $\varphi$ on $ABC$ such that
$$
\varphi(AA_1)=AA_2,\,\varphi(BB_1)=BB_2,\,\varphi(CC_1)=CC_2
$$
We may take $\varphi$ to be the $(BB_1\cap CC_1,BB_2\cap CC_2)$-isoconjugation.
:::

From Carnot theorem and Ceva theorem, the vertices of two cevian triangles are conconic.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Let $P_aP_bP_c$ and $Q_aQ_bQ_c$ be the cevian triangles of points $P$ and $Q$ with respect to $ABC$, then the points
$$
P_a,\,P_b,\,P_c,\,Q_a,\,Q_b,\,Q_c
$$
are conconic. This conic is called the **Carnot conic** (or **Cevian conic**) of $P$ and $Q$. The Carnot conic of $P$ and $P$ (which is tangent to the three sides of $ABC$ at the vertices of the cevian triangle of $P$) is called the **inconic** of $P$ (with respect to $ABC$). The $P$-anticomplement of the inconic of $P$ is called the **circumconic** of $P$ (i.e. the conic tangent to the three sides of the anticevian triangle at $A,B,C$).
:::
